analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal fracking rules on federal and tribal land wherever a state has any fracking rules.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the Interior Department from enforcing any federal rule on hydraulic fracturing in any state that has its own fracking regulations, and would order the department to follow state rules for fracking on federally owned land. It would also let Native American landowners consent to set aside federal fracking rules on trust land, require states to file their fracking rules with the federal government and make them public, and order a study of shale production's economic benefits. Because any state rule would displace the federal one, the practical effect would be to hand oversight of fracking on public land to the states alone.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal and Indian lands would deal with one regulator instead of two, avoiding federal chemical-disclosure and well-construction requirements wherever the host state has its own rules. State governments would gain final say over fracking even on land owned by all Americans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas producers on federal lands

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Interior Department from enforcing any federal fracking regulation, guidance, or permit requirement in any state that has its own fracking rules, leaving operators to satisfy state rules only.
Requires the department to defer to state permitting for all fracking activity on federal land, eliminating a duplicate federal review layer.
Blocks federal fracking rules on Indian trust land unless the individual beneficiary consents, giving Native American landowners the deciding voice there.
Orders a government study of revenue, jobs, and energy prices tied to shale production, and requires states to file their fracking and chemical-disclosure rules where the public can see them.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near wells on federal land, and the broader public that owns that land, would bear the risk of uneven state rules. There would be no federal minimum for disclosing fracking chemicals or for well standards, so protections would depend entirely on which state a well sits in.
analysis.who_pays_short: People near wells on public lands

drawbacks.text: Any state fracking rule would displace federal standards on federal land in that state, whatever its strength — so public lands would be protected only as well as the host state chooses, with no national floor.
The bill creates no federal requirement to disclose fracking chemicals; in states without disclosure rules, the chemicals pumped into wells on federal land could stay secret.

The good-faith case for the bill is that operators on federal land face duplicative state and federal permitting and that state regulators, with local geological knowledge, have overseen fracking for decades — but the bill settles that dispute by deleting the federal rules entirely rather than coordinating the two systems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The honest case for the bill is efficiency: one regulator instead of two, written by officials who know the local geology. But the design is lopsided — any state rule, however limited, erases the federal one, and the bill sets no national minimum for chemical disclosure or well standards on land owned by all Americans. The transparency provisions (states filing their rules publicly) and the GAO study are small offsets. On balance, the bill would trade federal oversight of drilling on public land for lower compliance costs for operators, leaving neighboring communities' protections to vary by state line.

outcome.mechanism: Sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and then its energy subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the two-year Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Flores introduced the bill on March 26, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day.
On June 5, 2015 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
It never attracted a single cosponsor in either party.
The bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the Interior Department's authority over fracking on federal and tribal land was left intact and operators got no relief from federal rules. The oil and gas interests the bill was written for gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Interior kept its authority; industry gained nothing

industries.note: Operators of wells on federal and tribal land would escape federal fracking rules — including any chemical-disclosure or well-integrity requirements — wherever the host state regulates fracking, cutting compliance costs. Geothermal developers on federal land get the same treatment. The savings come out of environmental oversight of drilling on publicly owned land.

States would become the sole fracking regulators even for federal land inside their borders, with no federal backstop — a permanent transfer of authority. In return, they would have to file their rules with Washington and make them public.
